prompt:
Write 12 short claim log entries (one to three sentences each) by an auto insurance adjuster for a parking lot collision claim, in time order. Injury: shoulder injury. The claimant is represented by a lawyer. Start each entry on a new line with 'Entry 1:', 'Entry 2:' and so on. No names, dates or amounts. (Internal reference C-1096; do not mention it.) Work these facts into the text naturally, in your own words, without listing them:
- The reported injury matches the kind and force of the crash well.
- Treatment followed a usual course and tapered off as the patient improved.
- No earlier injury to the same body area is known.
- Photos confirm some details, but there are no independent witnesses.
- The vehicle damage matches the described impact.
- The claimant later added small details, but the account stayed the same.
- It is not fully clear where in the vehicle the claimant was sitting.
- No earlier damage to the vehicle is known.
- Nothing suggests the damage happened before the coverage started.
- The driver is named on the policy.
text:
Entry 1: The insured reported a low-speed collision in a parking lot involving a single other vehicle, and the claimant has retained an attorney who has asked that all contact be routed through their office.

Entry 2: The driver is named on the policy and the coverage was in force at the time of the loss, with nothing suggesting the damage predates the policy start.

Entry 3: Photos taken at the scene confirm several details of the reported impact, though no independent witnesses have come forward to describe the collision.

Entry 4: The vehicle damage is consistent with the impact as described, and no earlier damage to the vehicle is known from prior claims or inspection records.

Entry 5: The claimant reports a shoulder injury from the collision, and the nature of the injury and the force involved in the crash appear to line up well.

Entry 6: Medical records show no earlier injury to the same body area, and no prior treatment history for the shoulder has been identified.

Entry 7: Treatment followed a typical course, with therapy visits gradually reducing as the claimant reported steady improvement.

Entry 8: It is still unclear from the statements and photos exactly where the claimant was seated in the vehicle at the moment of impact, and this has been noted for follow-up.

Entry 9: In a later conversation, the claimant added a few small details to the account of the collision, but the core description of events has stayed the same across each retelling.

Entry 10: The attorney's office provided a further written statement that echoes the earlier account, and no material inconsistencies have been found in the submitted records.

Entry 11: The file was reviewed against the vehicle inspection, the scene photos, and the treatment timeline, and the pieces are generally consistent with one another.

Entry 12: Pending receipt of the outstanding seating-position information, the claim remains open for evaluation under the bodily injury and property damage sections of the policy.
